passages.title: Hannah prays and dedicates Samuel
passages.summary: Hannah endures Peninnah’s provocation, prays at Shiloh, and later brings Samuel to serve there.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies Hannah's prayer during grief and her trust in God.

contextNote.title: A suffering woman's voice corrects a priest
contextNote.text: Eli first mistakes Hannah's silent prayer for drunkenness. Her explanation requires him to change his judgment. The book begins by exposing the limits of an established religious leader's perception.

passages.title: Hannah’s song and the failure of Eli’s sons
passages.summary: Hannah praises God. Hophni and Phinehas abuse their office. An unnamed messenger announces judgment against Eli’s household.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects Hannah's song with Jesus Christ.

contextNote.title: The household tests the meaning of sacred office
contextNote.text: Hannah's song celebrates reversals of status. Eli's sons use their position to take from worshipers. Their conduct gives the song's claims about power a concrete setting.

passages.title: Samuel hears the call
passages.summary: Samuel repeatedly mistakes the call for Eli’s voice. Eli guides his response, and Samuel receives a difficult message.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Samuel’s response with learning to recognize revelation.

contextNote.title: Receiving a call includes speaking difficult words
contextNote.text: Eli helps Samuel recognize the voice but must also hear its judgment. Samuel's first message threatens the household that raised him. The relationship joins dependence, teaching, and the duty to speak plainly.

passages.title: The ark is captured and Eli’s household suffers loss
passages.summary: Israel brings the ark from Shiloh into battle. The Philistines capture it. Eli and his sons die, and Ichabod is born.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church lesson examines trust in the ark. Why does carrying the ark fail to protect the army?

contextNote.title: A sacred object cannot secure a chosen outcome
contextNote.text: The leaders bring the ark after defeat, hoping it will save them. Its capture interrupts that expectation. The account separates God's presence from the people's ability to control a battle.

passages.title: The ark among the Philistine towns
passages.summary: The ark is placed beside Dagon at Ashdod. Distress follows its movement to Gath and Ekron.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects the ark’s troubles with Israel’s need to honor God.

contextNote.title: Power is questioned outside Israel's territory
contextNote.text: The captured ark appears to be a trophy at first. Dagon's collapse reverses the apparent relationship between conqueror and captive. The Philistine towns must interpret events they cannot control.

passages.title: The ark returns to Beth Shemesh
passages.summary: The Philistines send offerings with the ark on a cart. It reaches Beth Shemesh, where rejoicing gives way to mourning.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church lesson uses these events to study trust and obedience.

contextNote.title: The return includes a stated test of cause
contextNote.text: The Philistines describe how the cart's direction will distinguish possible explanations. Their uncertainty belongs inside the account. Sending the ark away is both an offering and an attempt to understand the distress.

passages.title: Samuel leads the gathering at Mizpah
passages.summary: The ark stays with Abinadab’s household. Samuel calls Israel to renewed worship and leads the gathering at Mizpah.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies turning toward God after earlier failure.

contextNote.title: A victory becomes a named act of remembrance
contextNote.text: Samuel places a stone and explains its name through received help. The object points backward to an event and forward to continued memory. This scene contrasts with treating the ark as a guarantee of victory.

passages.title: The people request a king
passages.summary: Samuel’s sons take bribes. Israel’s elders ask for a king. Samuel warns that kings take people, land, and goods.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church lesson invites readers to consider Jesus Christ as their King.

contextNote.title: A king can take what a people needs
contextNote.text: Samuel repeats what the king will take from households. Sons, daughters, fields, and animals all enter royal service. The people seek security through an institution that can also burden them. The warning does not disappear when a king is chosen. Read later royal success beside these costs.

passages.title: Saul searches for donkeys and meets Samuel
passages.summary: Kish sends Saul with a servant to find missing donkeys. Their search brings them to Samuel.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Saul’s selection with a call to service.

contextNote.title: A servant opens the way to royal appointment
contextNote.text: Saul's search appears to concern lost animals. The servant's advice takes him toward Samuel and a larger role. A person of lower household rank supplies the decisive practical suggestion.

passages.title: Saul is anointed and presented publicly
passages.summary: Samuel anoints Saul privately. Later, Saul is selected before the gathering at Mizpah and found among the baggage.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church lesson connects anointing and changed purpose with service by revelation.

contextNote.title: Public selection does not erase uncertainty
contextNote.text: Saul hides among the baggage when the assembly seeks him. His appointment also meets open criticism. The account gives the new king both recognition and a difficult beginning.

passages.title: Saul relieves Jabesh Gilead
passages.summary: Nahash threatens the people of Jabesh Gilead. Saul gathers help, wins the battle, and refuses to execute earlier opponents.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual studies Saul’s early leadership and the renewed kingdom.

contextNote.title: Victory gives Saul a chance to restrain revenge
contextNote.text: Some supporters want earlier opponents killed after the rescue. Saul refuses that demand. His first public success includes a limit on violence within the people he now leads.

passages.title: Samuel reviews leadership and covenant responsibility
passages.summary: Samuel asks the people to assess his conduct. He recalls earlier deliverers and warns both people and king to remain faithful.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual studies Samuel’s final address and continued prayer for the people.

contextNote.title: The outgoing leader invites public examination
contextNote.text: Samuel asks whether he has taken property or accepted bribes. This review contrasts with his earlier warning about royal taking. Both the new king and the people remain subject to covenant duties.

passages.title: Pressure at Michmash and Saul’s offering
passages.summary: Jonathan attacks a Philistine post. Saul’s men begin to leave. Saul offers a sacrifice before Samuel arrives. Samuel rejects his family’s lasting rule.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies obedience under pressure. The older manual also reads the offering as unauthorized priesthood action.

contextNote.title: Pressure reveals competing accounts of responsibility
contextNote.text: Saul explains his act through departing soldiers and Samuel's delay. Samuel judges it through the command Saul received. The dispute concerns who may decide that circumstances permit a changed duty.

passages.title: Jonathan’s attack and Saul’s dangerous oath
passages.summary: Jonathan and his armor bearer attack a garrison. Saul’s food prohibition places Jonathan under sentence of death, but the people rescue him.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual studies Jonathan’s faith and the harmful effect of Saul’s oath.

contextNote.title: The people challenge a royal sentence
contextNote.text: Saul's oath places Jonathan at risk despite his military service. The people refuse to let him die. Their intervention distinguishes the king's declared rule from a judgment the community will accept.

passages.title: Amalek, Agag, and Saul’s rejection
passages.summary: Saul attacks Amalek but spares Agag and selected livestock. Samuel rejects Saul’s defense and later kills Agag.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks why obedience matters more than making a religious display.

contextNote.title: Claiming a sacred purpose does not end the dispute
contextNote.text: Saul explains the preserved animals as intended offerings. Samuel challenges obedience expressed through a changed command. Read their disagreement beside the chapter's disturbing demand for destruction.

passages.title: David is anointed and enters Saul’s service
passages.summary: Samuel anoints Jesse’s youngest son David. David later plays music for Saul and serves in his household.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church lesson asks readers to consider a person's heart instead of outward appearance.

contextNote.title: Music belongs inside the court
contextNote.text: David enters Saul’s service through skill with music. His first task concerns the king’s distress, not public battle. That role brings him close to royal power before Goliath’s defeat. Music here is work, care, and a route into the household. Later conflict changes what that closeness means.

passages.title: David faces Goliath in the Valley of Elah
passages.summary: David brings food to his brothers. He accepts Goliath’s challenge and strikes him with a sling. He then uses Goliath’s sword.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how trust in God can give courage during a hard task.

contextNote.title: The chosen tools change the contest
contextNote.text: David declines Saul's armor because he has not tested it. His account of tending sheep supplies another kind of experience. The confrontation contrasts royal equipment with skill formed outside the court.

passages.title: Friendship, jealousy, and royal marriage plans
passages.summary: Jonathan forms a bond with David. Saul grows jealous, offers Merab, then arranges David’s marriage to Michal through a deadly demand.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church lesson compares Jonathan’s support with Saul’s jealousy.

contextNote.title: Public praise turns achievement into a royal threat
contextNote.text: The victory song compares Saul and David in numbered successes. Saul hears that comparison as a danger to his throne. Praise becomes part of the conflict rather than simple celebration.

passages.title: Michal helps David escape
passages.summary: Saul resumes attempts to kill David. Michal helps David through a window. David joins Samuel at Ramah, where pursuit is interrupted.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older Church manual compares Samuel's group of prophets with later Church schools.

contextNote.title: A daughter acts against her father's violence
contextNote.text: Michal's aid places household loyalty in conflict with royal demands. Saul's question exposes his expectation that she should assist him. David's safety depends on someone inside the king's own family.

passages.title: Jonathan warns David and renews their covenant
passages.summary: Jonathan tests Saul’s intent at the new-moon meal. He signals danger with arrows and parts from David in grief.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: What does Jonathan risk by protecting David from his father?

contextNote.title: Succession makes friendship politically costly
contextNote.text: Saul tells Jonathan that David threatens his future kingship. Jonathan still asks what wrong David has done. His question puts justice and friendship against his father's claim about family advantage.

passages.title: David seeks food at Nob and refuge at Gath
passages.summary: Ahimelech gives David consecrated bread and Goliath’s sword. Doeg observes him. David then escapes danger at Achish’s court.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects the bread account with Jesus’s later teaching about human need.

contextNote.title: Need tests the use of sacred food
contextNote.text: Ahimelech gives bread normally kept for sacred use. His questions still attach conditions to that decision. The scene places immediate hunger beside established religious practice.

passages.title: David gathers followers and Saul orders the Nob massacre
passages.summary: David gathers distressed followers and seeks safety for his parents. Saul orders the priests’ deaths. Doeg carries out the killing, and Abiathar escapes.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older Church manual condemns Saul's attack on the priests.

contextNote.title: Royal command does not make every action acceptable
contextNote.text: Saul's servants refuse to kill the priests. Doeg then performs the act they rejected. The account separates receiving an order from accepting responsibility for the act.

passages.title: Keilah, wilderness pursuit, and Jonathan’s support
passages.summary: David rescues Keilah, leaves after consulting God, and meets Jonathan during Saul’s pursuit. A Philistine attack interrupts the chase.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: How does David respond when the town he saved may hand him over?

contextNote.title: Rescue does not guarantee political loyalty
contextNote.text: David saves Keilah but learns its leaders may surrender him. The city's vulnerability complicates repayment through loyalty. Military service and secure refuge remain different things.

passages.title: David spares Saul in the cave
passages.summary: David cuts part of Saul’s robe but refuses to kill him. Afterward he speaks openly, and Saul acknowledges David’s future.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites readers to study David's self-control and forgiveness.

contextNote.title: Restraint supplies evidence against an accusation
contextNote.text: David uses the cut robe to show he could have killed Saul. The object supports his words more directly than a claim alone. His appeal asks Saul to judge conduct rather than fear.

passages.title: Abigail prevents David’s revenge
passages.summary: After Nabal refuses assistance, David prepares an attack. Abigail brings provisions and persuades him to stop. After Nabal dies, she marries David.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies restraint and forgiveness. It compares Abigail’s intervention with Jesus Christ.

contextNote.title: Wisdom stops violence before it gains praise
contextNote.text: Abigail intervenes while David prepares to kill the household's men. She speaks about his future and the burden of bloodshed. Her judgment protects people from a leader’s anger. David’s thanks does not make the original threat harmless. The account tests leadership through restraint, not only victory.

passages.title: David takes the spear and water jar
passages.summary: David and Abishai enter Saul’s camp. David again refuses to kill Saul, then confronts Abner about the failure to protect him.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies self-control. Restraint and continued separation occur together in the story.

contextNote.title: A second refusal also questions royal protection
contextNote.text: David again rejects killing Saul, then exposes the guards' failure. The spear and jar make his access visible. His restraint stands beside the court's inability to protect its own king.

passages.title: David lives under Achish and conceals his raids
passages.summary: David moves with his household and followers into Philistine territory. Achish grants Ziklag. David raids other populations and misleads Achish.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual links David’s raids with earlier commands to take the land. The raids also kill whole households.

contextNote.title: Safety under a patron depends on concealed violence
contextNote.text: David preserves Achish's trust through misleading reports of his raids. Killing potential witnesses protects that deception. The account complicates the fugitive's survival by showing who bears its cost.

passages.title: Saul consults the woman at Endor
passages.summary: Saul seeks help from a woman who calls on the dead. The chapter names Samuel as the speaker who warns him of defeat.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual says the speaker was not Samuel. The chapter itself repeatedly calls him Samuel.

contextNote.title: Saul seeks help from someone his policy endangered
contextNote.text: The woman fears the ban Saul himself imposed. His request requires secrecy and an assurance of safety. The king's desperation makes him depend on a practice he publicly rejected.

passages.title: Philistine leaders send David away
passages.summary: Achish defends David, but the other leaders distrust him in battle against Israel. David and his men are sent back.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: Why do the Philistine leaders distrust David, even though Achish trusts him?

contextNote.title: Suspicion prevents divided service in battle
contextNote.text: Achish trusts David, but the other commanders fear a change of sides. Their objection removes David from fighting against Israel. The account resolves his conflicting loyalties through others' decision.

passages.title: David recovers the captives and shares the spoil
passages.summary: David returns to burned Ziklag. An abandoned Egyptian servant guides the pursuit. David recovers the captives and gives equal shares to those guarding baggage.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: Why does David share recovered goods with people who stayed behind?

contextNote.title: Recovery creates a dispute about who deserves a share
contextNote.text: Some fighters exclude men who remained with the supplies. David treats their different work as part of the same effort. The resulting rule changes victory from a private reward into shared provision.

passages.title: Saul and his sons die at Gilboa
passages.summary: The Philistines defeat Israel. Jonathan and two brothers die. Saul falls on his sword, and the people of Jabesh Gilead recover the bodies.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: How do the people of Jabesh Gilead honor Saul after his defeat?

contextNote.title: An earlier rescue returns as care for the dead
contextNote.text: Jabesh Gilead retrieves the bodies after Saul's defeat. Its action recalls Saul's rescue of that town in chapter 11. The ending preserves gratitude after royal power and military success have ended.

events.title: Saul searches for donkeys and meets Samuel
events.summary: Kish sends Saul with a servant to find missing donkeys. Their search brings them to Samuel.
events.detail: Saul's search appears to concern lost animals. The servant's advice takes him toward Samuel and a larger role. A person of lower household rank supplies the decisive practical suggestion.

events.title: Saul is anointed and presented publicly
events.summary: Samuel anoints Saul privately. Later, Saul is selected before the gathering at Mizpah and found among the baggage.
events.detail: Saul hides among the baggage when the assembly seeks him. His appointment also meets open criticism. The account gives the new king both recognition and a difficult beginning.

lds.text: The Church lesson connects anointing and changed purpose with service by revelation.

events.title: Saul relieves Jabesh Gilead
events.summary: Nahash threatens the people of Jabesh Gilead. Saul gathers help, wins the battle, and refuses to execute earlier opponents.
events.detail: Some supporters want earlier opponents killed after the rescue. Saul refuses that demand. His first public success includes a limit on violence within the people he now leads.

lds.text: The older manual studies Saul’s early leadership and the renewed kingdom.

events.title: Samuel reviews leadership and covenant responsibility
events.summary: Samuel asks the people to assess his conduct. He recalls earlier deliverers and warns both people and king to remain faithful.
events.detail: Samuel asks whether he has taken property or accepted bribes. This review contrasts with his earlier warning about royal taking. Both the new king and the people remain subject to covenant duties.

lds.text: The older manual studies Samuel’s final address and continued prayer for the people.

events.title: Pressure at Michmash and Saul’s offering
events.summary: Jonathan attacks a Philistine post. Saul’s men begin to leave. Saul offers a sacrifice before Samuel arrives. Samuel rejects his family’s lasting rule.
events.detail: Saul explains his act through departing soldiers and Samuel's delay. Samuel judges it through the command Saul received. The dispute concerns who may decide that circumstances permit a changed duty.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies obedience under pressure. The older manual also reads the offering as unauthorized priesthood action.

events.title: Jonathan’s attack and Saul’s dangerous oath
events.summary: Jonathan and his armor bearer attack a garrison. Saul’s food prohibition places Jonathan under sentence of death, but the people rescue him.
events.detail: Saul's oath places Jonathan at risk despite his military service. The people refuse to let him die. Their intervention distinguishes the king's declared rule from a judgment the community will accept.
events.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual studies Jonathan’s faith and the harmful effect of Saul’s oath.

events.title: Amalek, Agag, and Saul’s rejection
events.summary: Saul attacks Amalek but spares Agag and selected livestock. Samuel rejects Saul’s defense and later kills Agag.
events.detail: Saul explains the preserved animals as intended offerings. Samuel challenges obedience expressed through a changed command. Read their disagreement beside the chapter's disturbing demand for destruction.
events.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks why obedience matters more than making a religious display.

events.title: David is anointed and enters Saul’s service
events.summary: Samuel anoints Jesse’s youngest son David. David later plays music for Saul and serves in his household.
events.detail: David enters Saul’s service through skill with music. His first task concerns the king’s distress, not public battle. That role brings him close to royal power before Goliath’s defeat. Music here is work, care, and a route into the household. Later conflict changes what that closeness means.
events.uncertainty: Named localities and broad regions only. Camp, cave, household, and road positions remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church lesson asks readers to consider a person's heart instead of outward appearance.

events.title: David faces Goliath in the Valley of Elah
events.summary: David brings food to his brothers. He accepts Goliath’s challenge and strikes him with a sling. He then uses Goliath’s sword.
events.detail: David declines Saul's armor because he has not tested it. His account of tending sheep supplies another kind of experience. The confrontation contrasts royal equipment with skill formed outside the court.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how trust in God can give courage during a hard task.

events.title: Friendship, jealousy, and royal marriage plans
events.summary: Jonathan forms a bond with David. Saul grows jealous, offers Merab, then arranges David’s marriage to Michal through a deadly demand.
events.detail: The victory song compares Saul and David in numbered successes. Saul hears that comparison as a danger to his throne. Praise becomes part of the conflict rather than simple celebration.

lds.text: The Church lesson compares Jonathan’s support with Saul’s jealousy.

events.title: Michal helps David escape
events.summary: Saul resumes attempts to kill David. Michal helps David through a window. David joins Samuel at Ramah, where pursuit is interrupted.
events.detail: Michal's aid places household loyalty in conflict with royal demands. Saul's question exposes his expectation that she should assist him. David's safety depends on someone inside the king's own family.

events.title: Jonathan warns David and renews their covenant
events.summary: Jonathan tests Saul’s intent at the new-moon meal. He signals danger with arrows and parts from David in grief.
events.detail: Saul tells Jonathan that David threatens his future kingship. Jonathan still asks what wrong David has done. His question puts justice and friendship against his father's claim about family advantage.

events.title: David seeks food at Nob and refuge at Gath
events.summary: Ahimelech gives David consecrated bread and Goliath’s sword. Doeg observes him. David then escapes danger at Achish’s court.
events.detail: Ahimelech gives bread normally kept for sacred use. His questions still attach conditions to that decision. The scene places immediate hunger beside established religious practice.

events.title: David gathers followers and Saul orders the Nob massacre
events.summary: David gathers distressed followers and seeks safety for his parents. Saul orders the priests’ deaths. Doeg carries out the killing, and Abiathar escapes.
events.detail: Saul's servants refuse to kill the priests. Doeg then performs the act they rejected. The account separates receiving an order from accepting responsibility for the act.

events.title: Keilah, wilderness pursuit, and Jonathan’s support
events.summary: David rescues Keilah, leaves after consulting God, and meets Jonathan during Saul’s pursuit. A Philistine attack interrupts the chase.
events.detail: David saves Keilah but learns its leaders may surrender him. The city's vulnerability complicates repayment through loyalty. Military service and secure refuge remain different things.

events.title: David spares Saul in the cave
events.summary: David cuts part of Saul’s robe but refuses to kill him. Afterward he speaks openly, and Saul acknowledges David’s future.
events.detail: David uses the cut robe to show he could have killed Saul. The object supports his words more directly than a claim alone. His appeal asks Saul to judge conduct rather than fear.

events.title: Abigail prevents David’s revenge
events.summary: After Nabal refuses assistance, David prepares an attack. Abigail brings provisions and persuades him to stop. After Nabal dies, she marries David.
events.detail: Abigail intervenes while David prepares to kill the household's men. She speaks about his future and the burden of bloodshed. Her judgment protects people from a leader’s anger. events.summary: David and Abishai enter Saul’s camp. David again refuses to kill Saul, then confronts Abner about the failure to protect him.
events.detail: David again rejects killing Saul, then exposes the guards' failure. The spear and jar make his access visible. His restraint stands beside the court's inability to protect its own king.

events.title: David lives under Achish and conceals his raids
events.summary: David moves with his household and followers into Philistine territory. Achish grants Ziklag. David raids other populations and misleads Achish.
events.detail: David preserves Achish's trust through misleading reports of his raids. Killing potential witnesses protects that deception. The account complicates the fugitive's survival by showing who bears its cost.

events.title: Saul consults the woman at Endor
events.summary: Saul seeks help from a woman who calls on the dead. The chapter names Samuel as the speaker who warns him of defeat.
events.detail: The woman fears the ban Saul himself imposed. His request requires secrecy and an assurance of safety. The king's desperation makes him depend on a practice he publicly rejected.

events.title: Philistine leaders send David away
events.summary: Achish defends David, but the other leaders distrust him in battle against Israel. David and his men are sent back.
events.detail: Achish trusts David, but the other commanders fear a change of sides. Their objection removes David from fighting against Israel. The account resolves his conflicting loyalties through others' decision.

events.title: David recovers the captives and shares the spoil
events.summary: David returns to burned Ziklag. An abandoned Egyptian servant guides the pursuit. David recovers the captives and gives equal shares to those guarding baggage.
events.detail: Some fighters exclude men who remained with the supplies. David treats their different work as part of the same effort. The resulting rule changes victory from a private reward into shared provision.

guides.title: 1 Samuel: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: A king can take what a people needs
steps.text: Samuel repeats what the king will take from households. Sons, daughters, fields, and animals all enter royal service. The people seek security through an institution that can also burden them. The warning does not disappear when a king is chosen. Read later royal success beside these costs.

steps.title: Music belongs inside the court
steps.text: David enters Saul’s service through skill with music. His first task concerns the king’s distress, not public battle. That role brings him close to royal power before Goliath’s defeat. Music here is work, care, and a route into the household. Later conflict changes what that closeness means.

steps.title: Wisdom stops violence before it gains praise
steps.text: Abigail intervenes while David prepares to kill the household's men. She speaks about his future and the burden of bloodshed. Her judgment protects people from a leader’s anger. David’s thanks does not make the original threat harmless. The account tests leadership through restraint, not only victory.

textRoutes.summary: Hannah endures Peninnah’s provocation, prays at Shiloh, and later brings Samuel to serve there.
textRoutes.detail: Eli first mistakes Hannah's silent prayer for drunkenness. Her explanation requires him to change his judgment. The book begins by exposing the limits of an established religious leader's perception.
